record.original_question: If the p-th powers in a finite p-group form a subgroup, must that subgroup be powerful? That is, for p ̸= 2, if the p-th powers in a p-group of exponent p2 form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian? For a 2-group of exponent 8, if the squares form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian?

evidence.quote: If the p-th powers in a finite p-group form a subgroup, must that subgroup be powerful? That is, for p ̸= 2, if the p-th powers in a p-group of exponent p2 form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian? For a 2-group of exponent 8, if the squares form a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Recall that a finite p-group G is called powerful if p is odd and [G,G] ≤ G^p (the subgroup generated by p-th powers), or if p = 2 and [G,G] ≤ G^4. Equivalently, for odd p a powerful p-group has an abelian quotient by G^p.

Consider a finite p-group G and let P(G) = { x^p : x ∈ G } denote the set of p-th powers in G. Suppose that P(G) is a subgroup of G (i.e., the set of p-th powers is closed under the group operation; in general it need not be).

(a) Must the subgroup ⟨P(G)⟩ = P(G) then be powerful?

(b) Equivalently, in the smallest interesting cases:
   (i) For an odd prime p, if G is a finite p-group of exponent p^2 and the set of p-th powers in G forms a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian?
   (ii) For p = 2, if G is a finite 2-group of exponent 8 and the set of squares { x^2 : x ∈ G } forms a subgroup, must that subgroup be abelian?

Determine whether (a), (b)(i), and (b)(ii) hold, or exhibit counterexamples.
